sources.title: Paul Sidwell, Classifying the Austroasiatic Languages: History and State of the Art
sources.note: Specialist history of Austroasiatic classification and disagreement over internal branching.

sources.title: Glottolog 5.3: Austroasiatic
sources.note: Current curated language-family entry and classification references.

sources.title: Paul Sidwell, The Austroasiatic Central Riverine Hypothesis
sources.note: Explicitly labeled linguistic hypothesis about homeland and dispersal, not a map of known Iron Age speakers.

sources.title: Roger Blench, Origins of Ethnolinguistic Identity in Southeast Asia
sources.note: Critical review of attempts to match language families, archaeology and population history.

sources.title: Charles Higham, Early Southeast Asia: From First Humans to First Civilizations
sources.note: Current archaeological synthesis of mainland Southeast Asian prehistory and early states.

sources.title: Charles Higham, Social Change in Southeast Asia during the Iron Age
sources.note: Regional Iron Age synthesis emphasizing varied local trajectories.

sources.title: Miriam Stark, Early Mainland Southeast Asian Landscapes in the First Millennium AD
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis of the long transition to cities, states and writing after this card interval.

sources.title: Dougald O'Reilly, Complex Society in Prehistoric Mainland Southeast Asia
sources.note: Overview of Bronze and Iron Age settlement, burial and social differentiation.

sources.title: Higham, Douka and Higham, A New Chronology for the Bronze Age of Northeastern Thailand
sources.note: Bayesian chronology and warning that regional phases remain debated.

sources.title: Higham and colleagues, Changing Social Inequality from First Farmers to Early States in Southeast Asia
sources.note: Quantitative mortuary analysis across the Ban Non Wat, Noen U-Loke and Non Ban Jak sequence.

sources.title: Castillo and colleagues, Social Responses to Climate Change in Iron Age North-east Thailand
sources.note: Archaeobotanical evidence for rice systems, chronology and later water management.

sources.title: Higham, Environmental and Social Change in Northeast Thailand during the Iron Age
sources.note: Regional sequence linking climate, houses, farming, infant mortality and later social change.

sources.title: McGrath and Boyd, The Chronology of the Iron Age Moats of Northeast Thailand
sources.note: Direct dating evidence that major ditch and moat works need not belong to the whole Iron Age.

sources.title: Higham and Higham, New Radiocarbon Dates for Iron Age Noen U-Loke
sources.note: Directly dated rice and detailed mortuary sequence at Noen U-Loke.

sources.title: Domett and Tayles, Human Biology from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age in the Mun River Valley
sources.note: Bioarchaeological evidence for health and limits of excavated cemetery samples.

sources.title: Newton and colleagues, Dental Health in Iron Age Cambodia
sources.note: Dental evidence from Phum Snay and Phum Sophy with cautious links to food and labor.

sources.title: Domett, O'Reilly and Buckley, Bioarchaeological Evidence for Conflict in Iron Age North-west Cambodia
sources.note: Skeletal trauma and weapons at Phum Snay, with contextual interpretation.

sources.title: Domett and O'Reilly, Health in Pre-Angkorian Cambodia
sources.note: Bioarchaeological analysis of excavated and rescued human remains at Phum Snay.

sources.title: Reinecke and colleagues, Early Cambodian Gold and Silver from Prohear
sources.note: Excavation, chronology, burial context and compositional study at Prohear.

sources.title: O'Reilly and colleagues, Airborne LiDAR Prospection at Lovea
sources.note: Later Iron Age settlement evidence used to prevent backdating visible moats and reservoirs.

sources.title: Berenice Bellina, Khao Sam Kaeo: An Early Port-city between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea
sources.note: EFEO research volume on chronology, settlement, crafts, environment and exchange.

sources.title: Murillo-Barroso and colleagues, Khao Sam Kaeo as an Archaeometallurgical Crossroads
sources.note: Technical analysis of metals, slags, crucibles, moulds and multiple metallurgical traditions.

sources.title: Lankton, Dussubieux and Gratuze, Glass from Khao Sam Kaeo
sources.note: Material analysis of glass working and transferred craft knowledge.

sources.title: Cristina Castillo, Archaeobotany at Khao Sam Kaeo
sources.note: Rice, cultivation weeds, imported plants and preservation limits from occupation contexts.

sources.title: Castillo and Fuller, Rice, Beans and Trade Crops on the Early Maritime Silk Route
sources.note: Direct archaeobotanical evidence for local foods and mobile crops at coastal exchange sites.

sources.title: Dussubieux and Bellina, Glass Ornament Production and Trade Polities in the Upper Thai Peninsula
sources.note: Elemental and technological analysis of early glass workshops at Khao Sek and Khao Sam Kaeo.

sources.title: Ian Glover, The Dvaravati Gap: Linking Prehistory and History in Early Thailand
sources.note: Ban Don Ta Phet evidence and the chronological gap before Dvaravati.

sources.title: Pryce and colleagues, Laos Central Role in Southeast Asian Copper Exchange Networks
sources.note: Lead-isotope, metallographic and compositional analysis of Vilabouly copper production and exchange.

sources.title: Cadet and colleagues, Late Prehistoric Copper Smelting in the Lao PDR
sources.note: Experimental reconstruction clearly separated from direct archaeological remains.

sources.title: Kovacheva and colleagues, Salt Production in Pre-Funan Vietnam
sources.note: Archaeomagnetic analysis of briquetage and brine-heating technology at Go O Chua.

sources.title: Campos and colleagues, In Search of a Musical Past at Go O Chua
sources.note: Microscopic manufacture study and cautious interpretation of antler chordophone candidates.

sources.title: Piper, Contextualising the Neolithic Occupation of Southern Vietnam
sources.note: Regional site sequence including Go O Chua settlement, burials, salt debris and grave goods.

sources.title: Vietnam National Museum of History, The Pre-Oc Eo Period in Southern Vietnam
sources.note: Institutional overview of southern Vietnamese burial sites and material connections.

sources.title: Lam Thi My Dung, Central Vietnam from 500 BCE to 500 CE
sources.note: Regional archaeology that keeps Sa Huynh and later Champa distinct from an Austroasiatic label.

sources.title: Lam Thi My Dung, Jar Burial Traditions in Prehistoric Vietnam
sources.note: Direct archaeological comparison of varied jar-burial traditions and debated connections.

sources.title: Higham, Mortuary Rituals and Social Change from the Neolithic to the Iron Age in Thailand
sources.note: Long mortuary sequence with children, adults, craft associations and later residential burial.

sources.title: Willis and colleagues, The Age-at-death Profile of Burial Sites in Mainland Southeast Asia
sources.note: Taphonomic and funerary cautions for interpreting infants, children and cemetery populations.

sources.title: Higham and Alves, The Southeast Asian Prehistoric House
sources.note: Archaeological and linguistic comparison, used with explicit caution against circular identity claims.

sources.title: Higham and colleagues, Excavation of Non Ban Jak
sources.note: Late Iron Age houses, floors, kilns and residential burials used only as later comparison.

sources.title: Lipson and colleagues, Ancient Genomes Document Multiple Waves of Migration in Southeast Asian Prehistory
sources.note: Ancient DNA from multiple sites showing population mixture without directly identifying language.

sources.title: McColl and colleagues, The Prehistoric Peopling of Southeast Asia
sources.note: Ancient-genome evidence for several population histories, not one replacement narrative.

sources.title: Kutanan and colleagues, Reconstructing Human Genetic History of Mainland Southeast Asia
sources.note: Modern and ancient genomic analysis emphasizing heterogeneity among present Austroasiatic-speaking populations.

sources.title: Manguin and Stark, Mainland Southeast Asia's Earliest Kingdoms and the Case of Funan
sources.note: Current reassessment of later first-millennium CE states and the dangers of back-projecting Funan.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Lost Kingdoms: Hindu-Buddhist Sculpture of Early Southeast Asia
sources.note: Museum synthesis distinguishing early exchange from later inscriptions, religions and named kingdoms.

sources.title: Miriam Stark, Foodways through Ceramics in Southeast Asian Archaeology
sources.note: Methodological guide to what pots can and cannot reveal about cooking and eating.

sources.title: Carter, The Production and Exchange of Glass and Stone Beads in Southeast Asia
sources.note: Review showing locally varied production and exchange rather than one simple foreign-transfer model.

sources.title: Cristina Castillo, Rice in Thailand: The Archaeobotanical Contribution
sources.note: Direct plant-remain synthesis and preservation cautions for Metal Age Thailand.

sources.title: Bentley and colleagues, Matrilocality during the Prehistoric Transition to Agriculture in Thailand?
sources.note: Isotope-based mobility hypothesis used only to show how carefully family residence must be inferred.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact id mon-khmer is retained, but its label is treated as an anachronistic linguistic classification rather than a self-named people or polity.
The only decoded feature is one huge polygon in world-bc200.json; it is absent from every other audited snapshot.
The polygon includes parts of lower Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, southern Vietnam and the Malay Peninsula while excluding several nearby regions and sites.
Named archaeological sites illustrate local evidence and are never assumed to share one language, ethnicity, religion, government or household system.
The card explicitly provides no written sample because no securely localized 200 to 100 BCE text can be attributed to the supposed Austroasiatic speakers.
Direct finds, experimental reconstruction, later comparison, linguistic hypotheses and genomic models remain clearly distinguished.
The 100 BCE endpoint is an atlas-layer removal, not a collapse or extinction; fell remains null and no automatic successor is invented.
